opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The trip really reshaped how I think about it. From the U.S., it's easy to picture "China AI" as one monolithic effort, maybe a few labs chasing American frontier models. On the ground it feels much more like a busy ecosystem. There are a lot of companies, a lot of very young and very talented researchers, and an intense, pragmatic culture of shipping things.

The biggest thing I came back with is that open models are central to their strategy in a way they aren't for most U.S. labs. Releasing open weights is how many Chinese labs build reputation, recruit talent, and get adoption around the world. That matters because open models become the default substrate that researchers and startups everywhere build on. If the best open models are mostly coming from China, that's a real kind of influence, even if the absolute frontier stays in the U.S.

On capabilities, I'd say the gap at the very top is real but narrower than many people in Washington assume. Compute is still their main constraint. Export controls bite, and you can feel it in how much effort goes into efficiency, in training, in inference, in squeezing performance out of limited hardware. But constraints also breed creativity, and some of the most interesting engineering ideas of the past couple of years have come out of that pressure.

So I don't really frame it as a race with a finish line. It's more like two ecosystems with different strengths. The U.S. leads on frontier compute and closed models, and China is very strong in open models, fast iteration, and deployment. My main worry, and the reason I keep pushing on this, is that the U.S. has under-invested in its own open model ecosystem. If we care about who sets the standards and whose models the world's researchers use, we need serious American open models, not just closed APIs. That's the part of the race I think we're actually at risk of losing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses U.S. open-model investment and AI competition, but does not identify worsening public opinion toward AI as a risk to progress.

r002.rationale: It says export controls constrain compute, but does not discuss uncertainty about how chip sales will affect the AI ecosystem.

r003.rationale: It describes companies, researchers, and startups, but does not say they have little influence over the highest-level U.S.–China race decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that the trip made me much less comfortable with the word "race," at least in the way it usually gets used in Washington and on Twitter.

When people say race, they picture two sprinters on a track, one clearly ahead, one behind. What I saw in China looked a lot more like two ecosystems evolving under very different constraints and optimizing for different things. On the US side, the frontier labs are chasing the absolute ceiling of capability, and they have the compute to do that. On the Chinese side, the compute constraint is real, you feel it in every conversation, so the energy goes into efficiency, into open weights, into getting models that are good enough and cheap enough out to a huge number of developers very quickly.

And the open-weight piece is the part I think Americans underrate. Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, the Zhipu models, they're not just research artifacts. They're the default starting point for a lot of people building things, including a lot of people outside China. If you go to a hackathon in Singapore or Berlin or even parts of the US, the model being fine-tuned is often a Chinese one. That's a form of influence that doesn't show up in a benchmark leaderboard.

What struck me on the ground was how pragmatic the researchers are. There's less of the existential framing you get here. The questions were about distillation, data, serving costs, how to train well on hardware that isn't the latest Nvidia part. Very engineering-minded. And honestly, a lot of them read everything coming out of the US labs in detail. The asymmetry is that the US side mostly doesn't read them back, or treats their releases as copies rather than taking them seriously as contributions.

So if I had to summarize: the US still has the lead at the very top, and I expect that to hold for a while because of compute. But the lead is narrower than the policy conversation assumes, the gap closes fast on anything that can be replicated, and on open models specifically, China is arguably ahead on momentum. I came back thinking the right response isn't to panic or to wall things off further. It's for the US to actually invest in its own open ecosystem, because if we don't, the global default will be set somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses U.S. AI policy and competition but does not identify worsening public opinion toward AI as a risk to progress.

r002.rationale: It describes Chinese compute constraints, but does not discuss uncertainty about how chip sales will affect the AI ecosystem.

r003.rationale: It describes developers’ use of open models, but does not say that people building or using technology have little influence over high-level U.S.–China decisions.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it less as a single race and more as a competition across several dimensions. There’s model capability, but there’s also infrastructure, cost, talent, and how quickly people turn these systems into useful products. Those don’t necessarily move together, and you can have different leaders in each.

I also think we should be careful about treating either country as one unified actor. Companies, researchers, and governments have different priorities. Open models complicate that picture further, because progress in one place can become a foundation for work somewhere else.

So the question I’d focus on is: who can consistently turn research progress into widely available, useful technology? A benchmark lead is meaningful, but it’s only one part of that.

r002.rationale: The response discusses several dimensions of competition but says nothing about chip sales or uncertainty about their ecosystem effects.

r003.rationale: The response notes differing priorities among companies, researchers, and governments, but does not say that people building and using technology have little influence over high-level U.S.–China decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I came away thinking that the framing of a single AI race misses a lot. There’s the competition to build the best models, but there’s also the question of who can turn those models into useful products and get them deployed broadly. Those aren’t necessarily the same competition.

I wouldn’t treat a short visit as a comprehensive picture of China. But my impression was that the ecosystem is very serious and very competitive. The U.S. shouldn’t assume that having an advantage in compute or frontier research translates into a permanent lead across everything else.

Open models make that particularly interesting. Improvements can spread across borders quickly, and teams can build on each other’s work even while their governments are competing. So I’d pay less attention to declaring one country the winner and more attention to where each ecosystem is making progress: research, infrastructure, talent, and adoption. You can lead in one and still have a lot of work to do in the others.
